prompt.context: Our client is a commercial airline that is planning to upgrade their on-board amenities during the next round of plane purchases. They have already decided to provide on-board wi-fi for their passengers and are considering adding individual entertainment screens for each passenger. They have asked Bain to evaluate the proposal.
prompt.question: What would you consider in your evaluation of the proposed individual in-seat entertainment system?

clarifying_info.q: What is the primary goal of the upgrade?
clarifying_info.a: Profit is the main goal, but the airline could also use it as a differentiator to attract more passengers or as a standalone revenue stream.

Let's examine one route as an example — it is a 4-hour direct flight along the East Coast. There are 4 flights a day, seven days a week. There is no direct competition for our client along this route.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average occupancy for each flight?
clarifying_info.a: You may assume each flight is 80% full.

exhibits.title: Customer Survey — Demand by Price Point
exhibits.shows: Results of a customer survey about the proposed on-board amenities, showing the number of passengers willing to purchase in-flight entertainment at various price points.

data.note: Figures represent number of passengers per flight (out of 240 average passengers) willing to use the service at each price

framework: Revenues: (1) Quantity — increase in total passengers from differentiation, number of passengers who would purchase the entertainment service (dependent on flight length and class); (2) Price — proposed price of the entertainment service
Costs: (1) Fixed — installation cost of the entertainment system per seat, depreciation period; (2) Variable — subscription/licensing costs for programming content
Company context: synergies with the wi-fi already being added (bundling opportunities), other alternatives to deliver entertainment
Competition: whether other airlines on the same routes offer similar services, and customer price expectations

questions.prompt: Calculate the fixed cost per plane per year for the in-seat entertainment system (ignore Wi-Fi costs since that decision is already made).
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two cost components: depreciation of hardware (300 seats × $15,000 ÷ 10 years) and annual programming subscription ($90,000/year). Wi-Fi costs should be excluded as already decided.

math.setup: Fixed cost per plane per year = (seats × install cost per seat ÷ depreciation years) + annual subscription

questions.prompt: Using the customer survey data (Exhibit 1), build a profit table for a single plane over one year and determine the optimal price for the entertainment service.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute total revenue per flight at each price point (price × customers), annualize (4 flights/day × ~350 days or 50 weeks × 7 days × 4 flights = 1,400 flights/year), then subtract fixed costs. Optimal price is $5, yielding positive profit. Candidate should ask about the number of operating weeks (50 weeks is acceptable).

math.setup: Annual flights = 4 flights/day × 7 days/week × 50 weeks = 1,400 flights/year. Profit/year = (price × customers/flight × 1,400) − $540,000
math.answer: Optimal price is $5/flight, yielding $216,000 profit per plane per year

questions.prompt: What alternatives to the in-seat entertainment system should the airline consider?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will propose a lower-capital alternative such as iPad rentals paired with a streaming app. Key points: significantly lower upfront cost (~$600/iPad vs $15,000/seat), easier to repair/replace, can be bundled with Wi-Fi, enables a frequent-flyer reward avenue by offering the app for free.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternatives could the airline use to deliver paid in-flight entertainment beyond the proposed fixed in-seat screens?

categories.name: Device-based alternatives
ideas: iPad or tablet rentals with a streaming app
Passenger BYOD (bring your own device) with an airline-provided streaming app
Laptop-friendly tray tables and power outlets to encourage personal device use

categories.name: Bundling and pricing models
ideas: Bundle Wi-Fi + entertainment into a single fee
Offer frequent-flyer reward redemption for free entertainment
Tiered pricing by content type (movies vs. live TV vs. games)
Complimentary entertainment for premium/business class passengers to justify fare premium

categories.name: Content and partnerships
ideas: Partner with streaming services (Netflix, Spotify) for branded in-flight access
License local or regional content for international routes
Offer advertising-supported free tier to maximize reach

recommendation: Recommend implementing in-flight entertainment via iPad rentals paired with the already-planned Wi-Fi, rather than the proposed fixed in-seat screen system
This approach reduces installation cost from $15,000/seat to approximately $600/iPad, lowers financial risk, and is easier to maintain and upgrade
risks: Passengers may prefer their own devices, reducing iPad rental uptake
iPads can be lost, stolen, or damaged, creating operational overhead
Programming subscription costs remain similar regardless of delivery method
next_steps: Pilot the iPad rental model on the 4-hour East Coast route at a $5 price point
Track rental uptake and passenger satisfaction to validate demand assumptions
Evaluate bulk iPad procurement and insurance/replacement cost to refine the business case
Assess potential to bundle the entertainment app with the frequent-flyer program
